Semi-autonomous state in northeastern [[Somalia]]. Puntland was formed in 1998 at a constitutional conference in Garoowe and is a federal member state of Somalia. Its capital is the city of Garoowe in the Nugal region, which had a population of 4,334,633 in 2016.

It is bordered by [[Somaliland]] to the west, the [[Gulf of Aden]] to the north, the Guardafui Channel to the northeast, the [[Indian Ocean]] to the east, Galmudug State to the south and [[Ethiopia]] to the southwest. The name derives from the [[Land of Punt]] in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] sources, whose location remains uncertain.

On March 31, 2024, the government stated that it no longer recognized the authority of the central federal government and would not take part in federal institutions. It said it would act independently until a federal government with a constitution agreed in a referendum in which Puntland participates is in place.

Life stage of holometabolous insects between larva and adult. Insects with complete metamorphosis pass through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and [[Imago|imago]] (adult). During the pupal stage, adult structures form from imaginal discs while larval structures break down, a process of [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] controlled by hormones such as juvenile hormone and ecdysone. Most pupae are non-feeding and largely immobile, although [[Mosquito|mosquito]] pupae are highly active. Pupae are largely defenseless, so species often use cocoons, camouflage or burial. The stage may last from weeks to years; monarch butterfly pupae last eight to fifteen days. Pupae in temperate climates usually overwinter, while those in the [[Tropics|tropics]] usually wait out the dry season. The adult emerges by splitting the pupal case, a process called eclosion.

Form of theater or performance involving the manipulation of puppets, inanimate figures animated by a puppeteer. Puppeteers use hands, arms, rods or strings to move the puppet. Hand or glove puppets are worked from inside, as Punch and Judy puppets are. Marionettes are suspended from strings and a control bar, while rod puppets have a head on a central rod with arms worked by separate rods. Some glove puppets, such as Japanese bunraku figures, require two puppeteers each. The art was first recorded in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] in the 5th century BC, and Egyptian figures worked by strings may date to 2000 BC. Puppetry occurs in almost all human societies, serving entertainment, sacred ritual, carnival effigies and social change.

Measure of the prices of specific goods in different countries, used to compare currencies' purchasing power. PPP is the ratio of the price of a market basket in one location to its price in another. It rests on the law of one price, which holds that identical goods should cost the same everywhere absent transaction costs or trade barriers. If a computer costs 500 US dollars in New York and 2000 HK dollars in Hong Kong, the PPP exchange rate would be 4 HK dollars per US dollar. PPP is used to compare [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]] and cost of living.

Study of mathematical concepts independently of any application outside mathematics. Research is motivated by intellectual challenge and aesthetic appeal rather than practical use, although results may later prove useful. The distinction dates to ancient Greece, but it was elaborated around 1900, after non-Euclidean geometries, Cantor's theory of infinite sets and paradoxes such as [[Russell's paradox]] required a renewed standard of rigor and axiomatic methods. Yet many pure theories later found applications. [[Isaac Newton]] showed that his law of universal gravitation implied that planets move in [[Conic section|conic sections]], curves studied by Apollonius, and the [[RSA cryptosystem]] relies on the difficulty of factoring large [[Integer|integers]]. Today the distinction is more a philosophical preference than a rigid division.

Catholic belief in a passing intermediate state after death, in which a soul is purified before entering [[Heaven]]. The analogy is dross being removed from gold in a furnace. In Catholic doctrine it is the final cleansing of those who died in a state of grace, leaving only the holiness needed for heaven; it differs from the punishment of the damned in [[Hell]]. Late medieval writers framed it with metaphors of time, place and fire, and art portrayed it either as a fiery punishment or as a joyful relinquishment of worldly attachments. The [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox churches]] have different formulations of an intermediate state, and most Protestant denominations reject the Catholic view. Concepts resembling purgatory exist in [[Judaism]], [[Islam]] and [[Hinduism]].

English [[Protestantism|Protestants]] of the 16th and 17th centuries who sought to rid the [[Church of England]] of what they regarded as Catholic practices. Puritans held Calvinist theology and covenant theology, and they were divided over church government between episcopal, presbyterian and congregational forms. By the late 1630s they were allied with commercial interests and parliamentary opposition to the royal prerogative, and they came to power after the [[English Civil War|First English Civil War]] (1642–1646). After the monarchy was restored in 1660, almost all Puritan clergy left the Church of England, and many joined Congregationalist and Presbyterian churches. Puritanism also played a significant role in the settlement of [[New England]]. The term began as a pejorative for groups considered extremist.

Color similar in appearance to violet light. In the RYB model historically used in the arts, purple is a secondary color made by mixing red and blue pigments. In the [[CMYK color model|CMYK]] model used in printing it is made from magenta and cyan, and in the [[RGB color model|RGB]] model used for screens it comes from mixing red and blue light. According to [[Color theory|color theory]], it is a cool color. Purple has long been associated with royalty, because [[Tyrian purple]] dye, made from the secretions of sea snails, was extremely expensive in antiquity. It was worn by Roman magistrates and became the imperial color of the [[Byzantine Empire]] and the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. Surveys in Europe and the United States associate it with rarity, luxury, ambition, magic and mystery.

Genus of [[Bromeliaceae|bromeliad]] plants, the sole genus of the subfamily Puyoideae. Its 226 species are terrestrial plants native to the [[Andes]] of South America and southern [[Central America]]. Many are monocarpic, with the parent plant dying after one flowering and seed production. The genus is commonly divided into two subgenera, Puya, with eight species, and Puyopsis, with the rest. Puya raimondii is the largest known bromeliad, reaching 3 m tall in vegetative growth with a flower spike 9–10 m tall, while most other species have flower spikes of 1–4 m. The name derives from an Indigenous Mapuche word meaning point. In Chile, some species, known locally as chagual, supply young leaf bases for salads.

Last emperor of China, reigning as the Xuantong Emperor of the Qing dynasty from 1908 to 1912. Chosen by [[Empress Dowager Cixi]] as successor to the childless Guangxu Emperor, he took the throne at age two, with his father as regent. After the Xinhai Revolution, an abdication edict allowed him to keep his title and remain in the [[Forbidden City]] until 1924, when a warlord expelled him to [[Tianjin]]. Japanese authorities installed him as chief executive of [[Manchukuo]] in 1932 and as emperor in 1934. Captured by the Soviet Red Army in 1945, he was later repatriated to China, held as a war criminal and granted amnesty in 1959 by the [[Chinese Communist Party]], which presented him as a model of successful reeducation. He worked as a gardener and researcher and wrote an autobiography. He was protected by [[Zhou Enlai]] during the [[Cultural Revolution]].

Game, problem or toy that tests a person's ingenuity or knowledge. The solver puts pieces together, or takes them apart, in a logical way to find a solution. Genres include [[Crossword|crossword]] puzzles, word searches, number puzzles and logic puzzles; their academic study is called enigmatology. Some puzzles arise from serious mathematical problems, and solving them can contribute to research. Impossible puzzles have no solution, such as the [[Seven Bridges of Königsberg]]. Mechanical puzzles include the [[Rubik's Cube]], logic puzzles include [[Sudoku]], and [[Jigsaw puzzle|jigsaw puzzles]] are assembled from interlocking pieces. Mathematical puzzles often involve BODMAS, an acronym for Bracket, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction, which sets the order of operations.

British multinational professional services network based in [[London]], one of the Big Four accounting firms with [[Deloitte]], EY and [[KPMG]]. PricewaterhouseCoopers operates in 149 countries with a workforce of more than 370,000 (FY 2024). Formed in 1998 by a merger of Coopers & Lybrand and Price Waterhouse, it shortened its trading name to PwC in 2010. It has been implicated in tax fraud and avoidance and fined for audits that failed to meet auditing standards. During the [[Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)|Russo-Ukrainian war]], it assisted Russian oligarchs in hiding their wealth and contributed to bypassing sanctions on Russia.

Capital and largest city of North Korea, on the Taedong River about 109 kilometers (68 miles) upstream from the [[Yellow Sea]]. It is a directly administered city with a population of 3,255,288 in the 2008 census. According to legend, it was founded in 1122 BC. It was the capital of the ancient kingdoms of Gojoseon and Goguryeo and a secondary capital of [[Goryeo]]. It became North Korea's de facto capital in 1948 and was devastated in the [[Korean War]] before being rebuilt with Soviet assistance. The 1972 Constitution made it the official capital. It is the country's political, industrial and transport center, and about 99% of its residents are members, candidate members or dependents of the ruling [[Workers' Party of Korea]]. Under [[Kim Jong Un]] a construction boom followed.

Russian Romantic composer, the first Russian composer whose music made a lasting impression internationally. He wrote the *1812 Overture*, a violin concerto, the opera *Eugene Onegin* and the ballets *Swan Lake*, *The Sleeping Beauty* and *The Nutcracker*. Although musically precocious, he trained for a civil service career, as Russia offered few musical institutions. He graduated from the [[Saint Petersburg]] Conservatory in 1865, and its Western-oriented teaching set him apart from the nationalist composers known as The Five. Depression and personal crises marked his life, including the death of his mother, a failed marriage and the collapse of his 13-year patronage by Nadezhda von Meck. His sudden death is generally ascribed to [[Cholera|cholera]], though scholars still debate the cause.

Structure whose visible surfaces are triangular in broad outline and converge toward the top. Its base may be any polygon, such as triangular or quadrilateral, and its sides may be smooth or stepped. Most of a pyramid's mass lies near the ground, which allowed early civilizations to build monumental structures. [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamians]] built the earliest pyramidal structures, ziggurats with receding tiers and flat tops, constructed by the Sumerians, Babylonians and Assyrians. In [[Egypt]], pyramids were built from about 2700 BC until around 1700 BC. The first, a step pyramid for Pharaoh Djoser, was designed by [[Imhotep]]. The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza is the only surviving structure of the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]]. The largest pyramid by volume is the Great Pyramid of Cholula in Mexico.

Mountain range in southwestern [[Europe]] that straddles the border between [[France]] and [[Spain]]. It extends nearly 500 kilometers (310 miles) from the Cantabrian Mountains to Cap de Creus on the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. Its highest peak is Aneto, at 3,404 meters (11,168 feet) in Huesca, Spain. The main crest forms much of the political divide, with the microstate of [[Andorra]] between the two countries. Historically, the Crown of Aragon and the Kingdom of Navarre extended on both sides of the range. The name may derive from Pyrene, a princess in [[Greek mythology]], or from a Greek word for fire, according to classical sources.

Iron sulfide mineral with the formula FeS₂, the most abundant sulfide mineral and the source of the nickname fool's gold. Its metallic luster and pale brass-yellow hue resemble [[Gold|gold]]. Pyrite is found in quartz veins, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, and coal beds. Its name comes from the Greek for a stone that strikes fire; it was used with [[Flint|flint]] to make sparks, a practice dating to [[Neanderthal|Neanderthal]] sites. Since classical times it has been used to make copperas (ferrous sulfate). Pyrite sometimes holds submicroscopic gold, known as invisible gold.

Fast-moving current of hot gas and volcanic matter, or tephra, that flows along the ground away from a [[Volcano|volcano]]. Pyroclastic flows are the deadliest of all volcanic hazards. They are produced by certain explosive eruptions and travel at extremely high speeds and temperatures, hurtling downhill or spreading under gravity. The denser particles form the flow, while lighter ashes and gases form surges. Some currents can cross water. The term *nuée ardente* (French for burning cloud) was used for the glowing flows of the 1902 eruption of [[Mount Pelée]] on [[Martinique]].

Group of rock-forming inosilicate minerals with single chains of silica tetrahedra. Pyroxenes have the general formula XY(Si,Al)₂O₆, where X is usually calcium, sodium, iron or magnesium, and Y is a smaller ion such as aluminum, chromium, magnesium or titanium. They are found in many igneous and metamorphic rocks, and pyroxene and [[Feldspar|feldspar]] are the major minerals in [[Basalt|basalt]], andesite and gabbro. The upper mantle is composed mainly of [[Olivine|olivine]] and pyroxene. Clinopyroxenes crystallize in the monoclinic system and orthopyroxenes in the orthorhombic system. The name comes from the Ancient Greek words for fire and stranger, because the crystals appear in volcanic lava and were once assumed to be impurities in the glass, though they formed before the lava erupted.

Greek king of the Molossians and of Epirus, and statesman of the [[Hellenistic period]]. He became king of Epirus in 306 BC at age 13 but was dethroned four years later, then regained the throne in 297 BC with support from Ptolemy I Soter. In the Pyrrhic War (280–275 BC) he fought Rome at the request of the Greek city of Tarentum, winning costly victories at Heraclea and Asculum, hence the phrase Pyrrhic victory. He took Sicily from [[Carthage]] but was driven out and returned to [[Italy]], losing his gains after the Battle of Beneventum in 275 BC. He seized the [[Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedonian]] throne in 274 BC and invaded the Peloponnese in 272 BC. An assault on [[Sparta]] failed, and he was killed in a street battle at Argos.

Ionian Greek philosopher and polymath who founded Pythagoreanism. Around 530 BC he travelled to Croton in southern Italy, where he founded a school whose initiates lived a communal, ascetic life. In antiquity he was credited with the [[Pythagorean theorem]], Pythagorean tuning, the five regular solids and the identification of the morning and evening stars as the planet [[Venus]], though historians debate which discoveries were his and which belonged to followers such as Hippasus and Philolaus. The teaching most securely linked to him is the transmigration of souls. His ideas influenced [[Plato]], and Pythagorean symbolism later entered [[Western esotericism]]. No authentic writings survive, and the ancient biographies are largely legendary.

Fundamental relation in [[Euclidean geometry]] between the three sides of a right triangle. The square of the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle, equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides, written a² + b² = c². The theorem is named after [[Pythagoras]], but the relation is older: the Mesopotamian tablet Plimpton 322, written around 1800 BC, contains entries that can be read as 15 Pythagorean triples, and Old Babylonian mathematicians used the rule widely. In [[Analytic geometry|analytic geometry]], the squared distance between two points in a Cartesian coordinate system equals the sum of the squared differences in each coordinate. The theorem has been proved in many ways, possibly more than any other mathematical theorem.

High-level, general-purpose programming language emphasizing code readability and simplicity. It uses significant indentation, an extensive standard library and garbage collection, and supports multiple paradigms with an emphasis on [[Object-oriented programming|object-oriented programming]] and dynamic typing. Guido van Rossum began it in the late 1980s as a successor to the ABC language. Python 3.0 was a major revision that was not fully backward-compatible. Optional static typing was added beginning with Python 3.5. The name refers to the British comedy series [[Monty Python]]. It is widely taught as an introductory programming language.

Group of walled city-states in present-day Upper Myanmar. They existed from about the 2nd century BC to the mid-11th century, a millennium that linked the [[Bronze Age]] to the classical states period. The Tibeto-Burman-speaking Pyu were the earliest inhabitants of Burma of whom records survive, settling the plains of the [[Irrawaddy River]]. Five major walled cities include Beikthano, Maingmaw, Binnaka, Hanlin and Sri Ksetra. Halin was the largest until about the 7th or 8th century, when Sri Ksetra, near modern Pyay, became twice as large and the most influential. Beikthano, Halin and Sri Ksetra are [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]]. Trade with [[India]] brought [[Buddhism]], and the Pyu script, based on Brahmi, may have been the source of the Burmese script. Invasions from the Nanzhao kingdom destroyed the city-states in the 9th century, and the Pyu were later absorbed into the [[Pagan Kingdom]].

Type of two-dimensional matrix [[Barcode|barcode]] whose name is short for quick-response code. It was invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara of the Japanese company Denso Wave to label automobile parts. Its square grid of black and white modules is read by cameras and decoded with Reed–Solomon error correction. A QR code can encode numeric, alphanumeric, byte and [[Kanji|kanji]] data, holding far more information than a standard barcode. Uses include opening a webpage, adding a contact, connecting to a wireless network and making a payment. During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], restaurants used QR codes for touchless menus.
